Remembrance

Why we pause, who we remember, and how we show respect.

20 minutes
Think, point, speak or watch.
Nobody is put on the spot.

How would you like to join in today?

Discussion / choices: Think quietly · Point or show thumbs · Speak or watch

Key idea: Every way of joining in is welcome. You can think quietly, point, speak, or watch.

Presenter: Welcome pupils calmly. Explain what will happen in the assembly, including the short silence later on, so there are no surprises.

02 / 10 · Autumn 2 · Week 2 · Remembrance

Why we pause in November

1.5–3.5 min

Tap the highlighted words to see why 11 November matters.

Remembrance is about people and the cost of conflict, not celebrating war.

At the on the of November 1918, the brought an end to fighting in the First World War.

TIME: 11 o'clock in the morning, when the guns fell silent.

DATE: 11 November 1918, after more than four years of war.

MEANING: An agreement by both sides to stop fighting.

Discussion / choices: 11th hour · 11th day · Armistice

Key idea: 11 o'clock on 11 November marks the 1918 Armistice, when people paused to remember those affected by war.

Presenter: Read the sentence aloud first, then tap each highlighted phrase. Point to the historical register image showing how real names and dates were recorded.

03 / 10 · Autumn 2 · Week 2 · Remembrance

Who do we remember?

3.5–5.5 min

War affects many lives. Tap each group to see who Remembrance includes.

Remembrance includes people from the past and people affected by conflict today.

Soldiers, sailors, air crew, and support staff from Britain, the Commonwealth, and allied nations.
Medical staff, stretcher bearers, rescue workers, and volunteers who cared for injured people.
Ordinary people and families whose homes, safety, or loved ones were taken by conflict.

Discussion / choices: Armed forces and support services · Nurses, medics, and emergency workers · Civilians, families, and communities

Key idea: We remember armed forces, medical and rescue workers, and civilians and families affected by conflict.

Presenter: Tap each card in turn. Emphasise that people from many backgrounds, countries, and roles served and cared for others.

04 / 10 · Autumn 2 · Week 2 · Remembrance

Why do people wear a poppy?

5.5–7.5 min

Does someone have to wear a poppy to show respect?

Red poppies grew on damaged ground after battles in the First World War and became a symbol of remembrance.

Discussion / choices: Yes, everyone must wear one · No, wearing a poppy is a personal choice · Respect is shown by how we treat people

Key idea: Wearing a poppy is a personal choice. We show respect through calm, considerate behaviour.

Presenter: Make sure pupils know nobody will be judged for wearing or not wearing a poppy.

05 / 10 · Autumn 2 · Week 2 · Remembrance

Remembering in our community

7.5–9.5 min

Where might you see a war memorial or plaque near us?

Each name carved on a local memorial belonged to a real person from that community.

Discussion / choices: In a park, square, or quiet local spot · At a station, hall, or school building · In all of these community places

Key idea: Local memorials sit in parks, squares, stations, and halls to remind us that history happened to real neighbours and families.

Presenter: Invite pupils to point or show thumbs. Keep discussion general and avoid putting anyone on the spot about family history.

06 / 10 · Autumn 2 · Week 2 · Remembrance

What happens during the silence?

9.5–12 min

Watch the scene. Pause at the prediction point and choose what helps the room stay calm.

Knowing what to expect makes a quiet pause easier for everyone.

Before the silence begins, staff explain how long it will last and what will happen. Pause here: what can a pupil do with their hands and eyes so the silence feels calm and manageable? Some pupils look down at the desk, some focus on one spot, and everyone keeps the room quiet for others. When the silence ends, staff thank the room and everyone moves on calmly.

07 / 10 · Autumn 2 · Week 2 · Remembrance

How you can take part comfortably

12–14 min

Tap each option to find a calm way to handle the quiet pause.

You do not have to think of anything sad or look at anyone else.

Discussion / choices: Look at one spot on your desk or the floor · Rest your hands still and count slow breaths · Step out quietly with staff if you need space

Key idea: Looking at one spot, breathing slowly, or asking quietly for space are all safe ways to manage the pause.

Presenter: Reassure pupils before Stage 8 that watching quietly or looking down at the desk is completely fine.

08 / 10 · Autumn 2 · Week 2 · Remembrance

Our shared silence

14–16.5 min

Choose the length of our pause, or tap Reveal quiet reflection.

We pause together in stillness. Nobody needs to speak.

Shared quiet reflection

02:00

Discussion / choices: 2:00 silence · 1:00 silence · 0:30 practice pause

Key idea: We pause to remember those who served, those who cared for others, and all whose lives were changed by conflict.

Presenter: Choose 2:00, 1:00, or 0:30 to suit the group today. Start and end the silence with a calm spoken cue.

09 / 10 · Autumn 2 · Week 2 · Remembrance

From remembering to how we act today

16.5–18.5 min

Tap the three ideas in order to connect Remembrance to daily life.

Some people feel reflective, and some just focus on staying calm. Both are normal.

Discussion / choices: CARE · PAUSE · RESPECT

Key idea: PAUSE → RESPECT → CARE. We pause together, show respect for others, and look after our community.

Presenter: Guide the group to build the sequence: PAUSE first, show RESPECT during the moment, and carry CARE into how we treat people.

10 / 10 · Autumn 2 · Week 2 · Remembrance

One way to show respect today

18.5–20 min

Choose the two actions that help everyone leave calmly.

Keep your choice private if you prefer.

Discussion / choices: Leave the hall calmly and give people space · Rush and talk loudly over others · Speak to a trusted adult if you want to talk

Key idea: Leaving calmly, giving people space, and checking in with a trusted adult if needed show respect for everyone.

Presenter: Thank the group for their calm focus. Remind pupils which staff are available if anyone wants a quiet chat afterwards.

Word help

remembrance
Stopping to think about people whose lives were changed or lost because of war.
armistice
An agreement to stop fighting. The First World War armistice began at 11 o'clock on 11 November 1918.
civilian
A person who is not in the armed forces.
memorial
A stone, plaque, or place that helps a community remember people.
symbol
An object or sign that stands for an idea, such as a poppy for remembrance.

Teacher desk

20-minute assembly · secondary SEMH

Participation and delivery

Read every prompt and option aloud. Pupils may answer by pointing, thumbs, speaking, or simply watching. Staff operate the board; nobody needs to type. Allow processing time. Do not require eye contact or invite personal disclosures.

Keep the tone calm, factual, and inclusive. Remembrance is about people and shared respect, not glorifying conflict. Wearing a poppy is a personal choice. Give pupils clear options for how to manage the silence, including stepping out quietly if needed.
